utterances.text: I don't know what ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the upper part of the statement, it says, "On the 30th of September."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you zoom in on to this part so that the witness can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's at the top of the statement.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: My husband went to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it says, "the 30th of September, 1994" at the top?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the second part of the statement, can you see that it says "statement"?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read part of your husband's statement which concerned the incident that you have spoken to us about and told us how it happened and of which you said that you spoke to your husband about. Your husband stated: "On the 2nd of November, 1994, at about 9.00, my wife, Ramiza, took -- went to the well, which is about 50 metres from our house. When she left -- when she got out of the door of the house -- "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know whether it's a translation problem, but the English translation was to the effect that it happened, the witness left at around 9.00. The English translation which came with the document indicates at around 10.00. And when I look at the original, it seems to be quite clearly 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't think that this is important, given that I said that in the statement it says 10.00. But in any event, it is in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think both the text as we have in front of us and the translation seems to relate 10.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to continue and read another two lines. "When she got out of the door, the house's door, she had a look in the direction of the aggressor's positions in Rajlovac, and she then heard a shot from the direction of the depot, and Ramiza was hit in the area of the left -- below the left knee." Witness, have you understood what I have just read out?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, I have. But I didn't go outside of the house. I had to go further away from the house in order to cross the road to go and get the water. When I was returning, that's when I was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did this incident take place in the morning, or was it in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go outside of the house and were you in front of the entrance to your house?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, I just had to -- yes, I went outside of the house and crossed the road and went to get the water. And I was returning with the water when I was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So this part of the statement given by your husband is not correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us where your neighbour Rasema lives?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: In the neighbourhood, maybe -- I don't know. What should I say? A bit further away from my house. We went to get water together. We always wanted to go together, to prevent someone from being alone in case something happened to someone. In such an event, they could be helped.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before, as you said, you were hit, so before being hit, did you always take that route to go to the well?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How often did you go there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: To fetch water?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Well, whenever necessary. Sometimes you couldn't -- you'd have to wait for 24 hours because there were queues and you wouldn't be able to fill your bucket up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And before you were allegedly wounded by this shot on that day, was there any shooting in that area and could you tell us whether someone else was wounded in this manner?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, but not on that day. Muharem Musanovic was wounded when he was going to UNPROFOR, when rubbish was being claimed because this is where rubbish was thrown away. UNPROFOR was there, and the Civilian Protection. They were cleaning away the rubbish, and Musanovic Muharem was hit by a sniper maybe about 50 metres further down from where I was hit. He was taken to a hospital. The UN took him to the hospital, but he died. And afterwards, Osmanovic Fatima, she was wounded in the head, and the bullet remained in her face. And then further down below where I was wounded when fetching the water, Mustafa Poljo was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any information on when these incidents happened? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: What do you mean, information? I saw that with my own eyes. I could see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you see that? When did this take place? Can you tell us what the year was and on what day?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Muharem was wounded before me. He was hit before me. He was hit, and he died. And Fatima was hit seven days after me. Poljo Mustafa, he was hit after me. I don't know when exactly. It was the war, and I couldn't remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether during that period in which these people were wounded, was there any fighting? Was there shooting in that area?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: No, no, there was no fighting. They were just snipers who would fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these incidents were reported to the competent organ or to the police?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I don't know. I know about Fatima and Muharem. But it must have been reported. She was treated in the hospital. It must have been reported. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the incident that happened to you, did members of the UNPROFOR come to visit you at the scene of the crime?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did they come to carry out an on-site investigation? Did the members of UNPROFOR come when, as you said, Fatima was wounded, too?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which hospital was Fatima admitted to? What kind of injuries does she sustain?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I think it was in the face, in her nose, and the bullet was lodged in her face. I just don't know what hospital she went to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does she live near you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: She does. But she died.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness the photograph 1812. It is the photograph which has pencil markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that 1811 or 1812? I see a photograph tendered by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1812.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please indicate? This morning, there was a document tendered by the Prosecution which bears 1811. But if you have another photograph in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is a photograph, Mr. President, which ends with 1-2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would you then please provide this photograph --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is that same photograph, Your Honour. It is the same photograph, 1811 and 1812. 1811.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We only received this morning 1811. If there is a 1812, I'd like to have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two numbers, 1812 and 1811, but they seem to be the same exhibit. There's a likely -- perhaps they are slightly different in these shaded, in these marked parts. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just have a look at the bottom. Are these numbers, that is 0212-4046, 0212-4046, is that the same number? Let me -- could you please, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I could assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The numbers on the bottom are not the same as I see. Yes, please, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could remove her headphones in Sarajevo, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Philpott, could you please assist the witness in taking off her headphones. Yes, please, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness a few moments ago referred to another incident where someone was shot in the same place, that is Fatima Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Indeed, that incident is number 17 of the scheduled incidents, and evidence will be called about that. One of the witnesses to that incident who will be called is Rasema Menzilovic, who was also mentioned this morning in this witness's evidence. She has made a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, and there is a copy of the same photograph attached to her statement. And that copy of the photograph is 1812. So I suspect that my friends have inadvertently picked up the photograph which was attached to Rasema Menzilovic's statement and confused it with the photograph which was given to them by us in relation to today's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And there are differences I think in the markings on the photograph. So 1811 is indeed the photograph which was attached to Ramiza Kundo's statement and which the Prosecution has sought to tender. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, first I'll return 1812 to you and also 1811, which was just provided to us. So if you want to -- the Prosecution has not presented as evidence photograph P1812. So if you want to do it after you heard the explanation of the differences between the two photographs, of course it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The photograph 1811, that is the photograph I want shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps, Ms. Philpott, could you please replace the headphones so that Mrs. Kundo is able to hear us. I have no picture on my screen -- yes, now I have the image of Sarajevo again. Ms. Kundo, we'll continue. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed. Could, Ms. Philpott -- no, the photograph is just here, not in Sarajevo. Could, perhaps, Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] I have a copy of P1811.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if you put it on the ELMO in Sarajevo, that would be the most convenient, I think, Ms. Philpott. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kundo, do you have before you the photograph which you identified as the photograph depicting your house?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: No, it's not my house. It's my neighbour's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you sign this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, can you tell us where did you put your signature on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Where I sign it, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you signed this photograph, did it already have these black lines?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All he did was show it to me. I don't know if I signed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps again the witness might remove her headphones very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Philpott, could you please take off the headphones of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The reverse of the photograph that was shown -- excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, the original photograph that was attached to the statement indeed bears the signature of the witness and the date and that of the investigator and that of the interpreter. It's placed on the reverse of the photograph. I'm happy for my learned colleagues to see that. The reverse was not given to the Defence. That is because of some budgetary constraints that we are under in terms of making the reverse of the photographs available. But I should make that clear at this stage where inadvertently my learned colleagues misrepresent the situation. So I'm happy for my friends to have access to the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you'll first, Mr. Usher, show the original to the Defence so that they can see what is on the back. On the other hand, Mr. Ierace, since the back of the photograph seems to have some relevance as well, since part of the statement of the witness was about signing a photograph, I think it would be proper - well, whether there are any budgetary restraints or not - to provide both sides of a document if both sides are relevant. Of course, I'm not asking you to copy every back page of any document, but here it seems to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I entirely agree, Mr. President. And in future we will at least make available some black and white copies of those details, if not colour. I have some black and white copies here now should you, Mr. President, or Your Honours, or the Defence wish to have those copies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic. Did I understand, Mr. Ierace, that you have copies of the back part available so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Black and white copies, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that at least the Chamber can also have a look at the other side. Mr. Ierace, wouldn't it be proper to tender the double-sided black and white copy as perhaps a similar number?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's what the Chamber expects the Prosecution to do. And Ms. Pilipovic, when questioning the witness about her signature, would you please take care that the witness is not going to be confused about the absence of a signature when the signature is on the back. So if you're asking her to tell us where her signature is, that you show her both sides, perhaps through the ELMO, of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst I'm on my feet, in case it becomes relevant during the remainder of the cross-examination, may I inform you that the exhibit number for the statement dated the 4th of May, 2001 by this witness is P3673.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a moment. P3673. Yes. And the 30th of October?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Ms. Pilipovic, do you think that the headphones could be replaced, or is there anything else you'd like to bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, she can have the headset back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Philpott, could you please have the headphones replaced. Ms. Kundo, I take it that you can hear us again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, as a matter of fact, I'd like that the photograph be shown, 181A, because I have some questions I want to ask with regard to this photograph. 1812A?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not yet. You have to provide the copies, and because it has not been -- we haven't seen it until now. So if you want to tender that, either you prepare copies or --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. In that case, we can use the 360-degrees photograph, because these photographs can also be seen on the circular photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then could please 3279V be played. Ms. Philpott, can you confirm that the 360-degrees photograph is on the screen in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, Your Honour. We have the image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us on this photograph, the hill that one sees in the background, what is the name of that neighbourhood, of that locality?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: It's Brijesce Brdo Cikma. That is how it was. Now it's Bulbulistan.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, 1993, 1994, who had this hill under control? Was it the BH army or the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters, however, asked the last answer to be repeated by the witness. Ms. Kundo, the last question put to you was: "In 1992, 1993, 1994, who had this hill under control? Was it the BH army or the army of the Republika Srpska?" And we could not hear your answer. Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our army controlled our neighbourhood, and those other hills, those other hills were held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ierace, is there any need for re-examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. And I would seek your leave to ask one further question in chief. But perhaps I could first ask the questions arising from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mrs. Kundo, you mentioned three other incidents which took place in the same area where people were shot. One of those was Muharem Mesanovic, and you said that he was --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Mesanovic. No, Mesanovic, I think. "M-E."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said that he died -- rather, he was shot before you were shot. Approximately how long before you was he shot?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I would say perhaps -- I don't know. No, I can't say really. I don't know. I don't want to be wrong, but it could have been - I don't know - five, six months. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You've told us that you were shot in November of 1993. Are you able to say whether he was shot in 1993 or earlier?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I think it was earlier. Was it that same year or not? I don't know. All I know is that it was before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You also mentioned another -- the name of another person who was shot, Mustafa Poljo. You said that he was shot after you. Can you tell us approximately how long after you he was shot?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I think it was in 1994, so was it a year or less after me? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Haska Dudevic was another woman who was hit. She was hit in June 1992. She had gone with me to the spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kundo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that completes the questions arising out of cross-examination. I now seek leave to ask some further questions in chief which relate to the occupation of the witness and the identification of her occupation in the medical letter of discharge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please put the questions to the witness, and I'll ask her not to answer immediately so that the Defence would have an opportunity, although they do know by now what type of question it will be. If there's any objection now, could you please inform the Chamber then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President. We are talking about the medical documentation -- medical document and a photograph, and I'm looking at the transcript. I do not know if -- I need to confer with my colleague. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If it assists, Mr. President, I will confine it to one question as to her occupation at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. May I ask some questions of the witness relative to the medical documents that we saw a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you that you indicated that you would split up your cross-examination. So I was a bit, when Ms. Pilipovic said that -- what did she exactly say? That this would conclude the -- let me just have a look. I asked her to repeat her last answer, and just before -- yes, Ms. Pilipovic, you said that the Defence had no further. I now understand that the situation was that you had no further questions, and since it was indicated that Mr. Piletta-Zanin would also ask some questions, I suggest that we then perhaps first resume the cross-examination. And if you would meanwhile think about the request of Mr. Ierace to put one additional question to the witness concerning her occupation. Yes, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, proceed. Mrs. Kundo, now some additional questions will be put to you by co-counsel for the Defence, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. There was some confusion as to whether all questions of the Defence had already been put to you or not. Mr. Piletta-Zanin will now put questions to you. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Usher, could we have this on the ELMO, please. This is Exhibit P1800. It is the letter of discharge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, on P1800, we have two different versions, or the same versions, but could you please indicate whether you'd like to have the first page of that exhibit where there is an ERN number at the top or the second page which bears an ERN number at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall start with the first page. The first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know if we can all see it. Witness, can you see it? Can you see this document, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to be sure that we've got the right copy on the ELMO, could you please move it a tiny little bit downwards, Mr. Usher. Yes, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, usher. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you can see this document, and for the transcript, I'm saying that this is the first document of 1800. Will you please look and read very precisely, please, the name of the head of the hospital Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which is in the right hand corner, in the last box after the text which is printed. And I want you to read to us very precisely what you see.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Let me just read this. The doctor's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please read the name, the typewritten name, of the doctor? Witness, will you please read out what you see there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: "Head of the second ward, Lahovic." That is what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, Witness, only the name of the doctor whose name appears in this box. And can we zoom in this box so as to make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object. I object on the basis of relevance. The question seems to be a test of the witness's ability to read the document. If this goes to Mr. Piletta-Zanin's ongoing objection and complaint about the legibility of documentation, then this is not the way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please respond and tell us what the relevance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. President, because we think that other documents were given for this witness which were translated, and the translations on which -- the translations can in no way correspond to the text which was disclosed. But could the witness please take off her headphones? If I have to answer in detail, then I would like the witness -- I'd rather that the witness could not hear what we are saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a lot of Ps in both names. Ms. Philpott, would you please take the witness's headphones off. Yes. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, having regard to what Mr. Piletta-Zanin has just said, surely the only relevant question he could ask of this witness is which documents, if any, did you provide to the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first see whether his question was relevant or not. And I see that both parties assist each other in formulating the right questions to the witness, which is, I think, not the way to do it. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you asked the witness to read what she sees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'd like the witness to read what she sees very clearly because what we have here under Rule 65, we see something else. We wanted the witness to read what she sees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you're referring to translations, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We don't need the witness to read what is in here whether or not to find out. I mean, I expect that - dependent, of course, on the quality of her sight - that she could not read anything else which this Chamber would read. So I do not see what's the relevance of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have -- I have another line of questioning. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the objection is sustained as far as reading the text of the document it is concerned since you did not give any relevance to that. Then please proceed with your next question. Ms. Philpott, could you please replace the headphones of the witness. I have no image of Sarajevo at this very -- yes. We see that the headphones are replaced. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I see that we once again see this document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, this document, did you also sign this document? Did you put your signature on this document at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I don't know. I guess I did. I don't know. Is it there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How can my learned colleague ask this witness, is your signature there, when it is obvious to him that she cannot see half the document because it is on an ELMO in The Hague, not in Sarajevo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think you're fully aware of the problem raised by Mr. Ierace. Would you please keep that in mind when you continue your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This is the reason for which we were opposed to videolinks. Please, could you ensure that the totality of the document is legible by looking at the screen. Thank you. A bit further up, please. There we are, thank you. Just a bit further up, please, for the Prosecution. [In English] Okay, so that we can see everything. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I was informed that the P1800 document is available in Sarajevo. So I'd prefer it to be placed on the ELMO there because it's clearer for the witness. Ms. Philpott, could you please put the first page of -- yes, that's the one, I think. Could you just move it so that we can see the top and see whether there's an ERN number at the top. Yes, we can see it is. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that everything is clear for everyone now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, this document, do you remember having signed a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I did. I don't know. When they discharged me from the hospital perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for this answer. Does this document contain a second or a third or perhaps other pages, too?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I think that there was only the one page, the page that they gave me when they discharged me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Given that you have this document in front of you now, which is from the Prosecution, at the bottom of this document, and I am being very specific, I said at the bottom where we can read -- where we could read something if it was zoomed in on, at the bottom of this document, can you see, can you read the signature of a doctor whose name would be Kule something Ovic. "K-u-l-e," and then there's a blank, and then "O-v-i-c."

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, could you -- I would be grateful if the technician could make the entire document legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Could you zoom on -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, you can see this document. Can you show us, at the bottom of this document, where this doctor's signature is.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I would like to ask you to read what you have just pointed to with your finger. Could you read out the name of this doctor, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: It says Kupulovic, I think, but I don't know. It has been printed "Abdica," and then "Kulevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for having read "Abdic." So Madam Witness, it is not the name of Dr. Kupulovic, I think. Where did you see at the bottom of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we fully understand the kind of objections you have against especially the way this document is translated. This is not the way. I mean, we could ask -- if we wait for another second, you'll ask her to check whether the English translation is correct or not. I mean, would you please stop putting questions to the witness concerning problems that everyone in this courtroom might understand, but the only one who has not a slight idea of what it is all about, almost for certain, will be the witness. So unless you indicate that the witness is aware of these kind of problems and why you assume that she is, I'll prevent you from continuing this line of questioning. So if you want to explain this to us why you think the witness would have any knowledge of it, please go ahead. We'll then ask the witness to have the headphones taken off. If not, take whatever other issue you'd like to touch upon during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have one last question with regard to the doctor, and I would be grateful if the witness could reply. Was she treated in the hospital by a certain doctor? And I'm just going to check the name in order to make everything clear. Ivanisevic. Mr. President, I don't know if the witness heard me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we had forgotten to ask her to put her headphones on again. Ms. Philpott, could you please replace the headphones for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they are on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, were you seen by a doctor named Ivanisevic in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the name of the doctor who examined me and who cleaned my wound on the following day. I didn't know him at all and I don't know what his name was or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam Witness, what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I'm a housewife.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam Witness, what is your exact address?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: My address: Bulbulistan 52. Before, it was Brijesce Brdo Cikma 8A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just speak to my co-counsel for 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This line of questioning has been completed, and I think that the Defence has now finished with its examination with regard to this document. It will return to it at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could I now ask that one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was your occupation on the day you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I was a housewife. A housewife.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Kundo, I have a question for you in relation to a photograph that has been shown to you before. Could please the Document P1811 be placed on the ELMO. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Kundo, you gave testimony that the markings on this photograph were not made by you, but by a Robert or Barry.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give instructions to him in relation to these markings?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was you who indicated to him which parts of the building were newly constructed?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was you who indicated where the garage used to be?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "more or less"?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: I meant more or less, something like that. That where the garage was, we can't designate the place exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say that it is an indication which might not be an indication with extreme precision.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZA KUNDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers. Mrs. Kundo, this concludes your examination as a witness, I would say in this Court, but of course you're at a long distance from the Court. But nevertheless you are with us. We can see you; you can see us. Thank you very much for coming and giving your testimony because it's important for the Judges to hear the answers to the questions put by the parties and by the Judges in order to prepare the decisions we'll have to take. Thank you very much for coming. And Ms. Philpott, could you please then escort the witness out of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before asking Ms. Philpott to bring in the next witness, which is a protected witness, Mr. Ierace, Ms. AF, or E. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: AE, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's AE. I'd like to indicate that perhaps we'll take the decisions on the documents after the break. I cannot exclude that we need an exchange of views within the Chamber before we give final decisions on that. So perhaps we could now resume the -- that you now call the next witness, and that the witness will be examined. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Not just with regard to what we have just seen, but Defence also has objections with regard to the addition of these documents, both the medical documents and the photographs, because they hadn't been disclosed to them in their entirety according -- in accordance with Article 65. And also to the videocassette, the videocassette that we have just seen, and the reason is the one that I mentioned earlier on. It has to do with the chronology and the fact that the investigator, what he said, Mr. Robert Barry, because when what he said -- when he said what he said was before the hearing and before this hearing, one presupposed the existence of a shot wound. But the Defence was not present in order to outweigh this, to present an objection to this. And I mention this because I don't think it was clearly stated before. We have a chronological problem here since the contents of the cassette was entirely referred to in the entirety of the debate. And that is the problem that I want to mention with regard to all the cassettes which have to do with this presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as it happens, the Defence was present during the filming of this incident. I was with Mara Pilipovic around the corner whilst the camera was running. And that was one of a few incidents that we attended. I explained to her the procedure which was adopted during the filming, which was that neither I nor any other lawyer would be present during the filming. So she and I therefore absented ourselves from earshot and sight of the witness and the other -- the investigator and the camera operators at the critical time. Following the filming, she and I were then summoned to the scene, and Ms. Pilipovic was provided with earphones and she was given a screen, and she then viewed the video which had just been shot. So she viewed it within something like ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is the recollection of the -- no, no, no, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Ms. Pilipovic, is the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my respected colleague just mentioned a working day of ours in Sarajevo, and the two of us were not present when the witness was spoken to, the witness who gave testimony today. We were not present when this video was recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both of you or neither of you?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "both of us," I'm referring to my colleague and myself. Other members of the team were present, and the investigator with the witness who has been heard today. My colleague Ierace and myself did not observe that part. We did not observe the filming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that there's a contradiction. I don't know whether it's wise to continue this because it might not be that relevant. But perhaps you try to find common memories on visits abroad for you and for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I won't pursue it, Mr. President. But coming back to the tender of the material, at a time which is convenient to you, I will provide an explanation of the various medical reports. There is now material before the Trial Chamber through this witness which should make that quite clear to the Trial Chamber. That explanation will take about three minutes. I'm happy to do that whenever the material is tendered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me then just ask you another question in respect of the video, because I think it's now the second time that you are objecting on the basis of the chronology. Am I right in understanding that the picture was taken in October 2001?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't remember the exact date of the recording. But are you referring to -- I don't know the exact date for the video, but I could find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I know is that there have been tendered two documents, statements of the witness. One is from May 2001; the other one is from October 2001. Was the video taken in October? It was on the beginning of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think it was September, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, after May.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, September 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'm just trying to find out, is it the case of the Defence, before we give a decision, is it the case of the Defence that this witness was not hit by a bullet?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence contests these facts because, quite simply, no evidence was provided to it on this. So it contests the idea that there was a wound inflicted by a bullet, to use your terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I heard in evidence today as the testimony of this witness that she was hit by a bullet. So I do not clearly -- and I didn't hear any question during cross-examination as to contest that she was hit by a bullet. So it surprises me, at least, that the Defence now says that there's no evidence whatsoever and that it's contesting --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't I expect then questions put to the witness whether she was telling the truth when she said she was hit by a bullet? I mean, if you contest it, if there are no questions about it, then of course the Chamber might assume that the witness was telling the truth during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps we weren't quite clear. But I may have remarked that we tried to ask Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. questions about the area where her wound was inflicted on her. We raised the matter of a document which said that I was wounded, on the one hand, in the left leg, and on the other hand, a document saying that it was the right leg. I think that we asked this witness enough questions in order to put the witness's credibility into question. If the witness was wounded, that's one thing. But we say there were documents which said "wounded in the left leg," others which say "wounded in the right leg." So the Defence simply has no other choice but to say that we contest this. And I think that I tried to interrogate, examine the witness, with regard to the location of the wound, and this is what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're contesting what was the location of the wound. Okay, we'll keep this all in mind when we'll consider the objections. Mr. Ierace, I think we perhaps have the break first, but we have still three minutes. So if you would use the three minutes you indicated you would need to explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I could, Mr. President. The alternative would be to leave the tendering of this material until Monday so that we could make the most of our videolink time to finish Witness -- to do Witness AE and finish Witness AE today. I'm in your hands on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a matter of fact, since the witness is not available any more anyhow, Ms. Kundo, that we perhaps now proceed with Witness AE, but perhaps nevertheless have a break first. Let's then resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope that both parties were informed that we would be able to continue today. I saw the indication on your list, Mr. Ierace, that the next witness would take approximately one hour. So that we can continue until rather late in the after -- I'm aware of your being not present, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. But I expect, apart from your absence, that both parties will be able to continue this afternoon until we've finished Witness AE.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is true for the Prosecution, Mr. President. Mr. Stamp will be taking the next witness, and he is feeling confident that the examination-in-chief will be less than an hour. If we are to go to straight to Witness AE after the break, then assuming that this material will be tendered on Monday, might I be excused from the rest of today's proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we'll take our time next Monday to see if there is any ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I expect that it would continue for more than an hour after the break, I think it would be better for everyone to have a break of half an hour now so that we resume at 1.00, and that hopefully we'll end by 2.30 or anything between 2.30 and 3.00. Yes. Then we'll adjourn until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the next witness you'll call is a protected witness, AE.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: AE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the protection measures ordered were a pseudonym and face distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Face distortion. Let's just see whether it's effective at this very moment. Ms. Philpott in Sarajevo, are you there?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please guide the witness into the Court videoroom in Sarajevo. And we'll check whether the face distortion is effective at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will not call you by your own name, since protective measures have been granted in respect of you. I'll just verify that the facial distortion is effective, and I'll call you by the name "Mrs. AE." Mrs. AE, before giving testimony in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration. The text will be handed out to you by the representative of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. AE. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. AE, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first questions I'd like to ask are related to a document which identifies her for our records. And as the document has her name and date of birth on it, I respectfully ask if we could go into closed session just for that document to be given to her. It is marked P3672.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Philpott.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] I was not provided with that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not ... Does this mean that you have not Document P3672 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may I ask the technicians whether if we put something on the ELMO here so that it is readable in Sarajevo, whether this could be done without ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are we in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not in private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand, could it be confirmed by the technical booth that this picture does not go to the outside world?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is confirmed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's confirmed. Yes. So please proceed, Mr. Stamp. This was arranged with the technicians before, that whatever document would be on the ELMO of a personal nature would just be for us and not for the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness AE, I'm going to ask you to have a look at that document, and without telling us what is written, just answer two questions for me yes or no. Do you hear me and do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the document which you see there, do you see your name written on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you see your date of birth written on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then it can be taken from the ELMO and returned to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness AE, do you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For how long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Since 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it you lived there during the conflict between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And during this conflict, could you say in what district or community in Sarajevo you lived at, without telling us your address?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I lived at Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what was your occupation during this period that I just referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I am a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really very sorry, but I see that the question covers 1995, 9-5, and this goes beyond the time frame of the indictment. And therefore, is it relevant to these proceedings? I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just merely asked her where she lived between 1992 and 1995, just to narrow down a period of time. I will get narrower as time goes by in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, during the period of this conflict, did you always have drinking water running in the pipes and taps at your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in those circumstances, how did you get drinking water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: We went -- at times it would take us half an hour on foot, and under gunfire, we had to go to people who had their water pumps, until the neighbourhood community organised a supply of water or until they found some water and set up some water pumps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, briefly, during the period from September 1992 to August 1994, what were the circumstances in respect of the conflict in Dobrinja? Was there shelling and sniping in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Day in, day out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did this -- and could you tell us what type of people this shelling and sniping affected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I wish to take you to the 12th of July, 1993. In the morning of that day, can you recall where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I do remember it. I was at a water pump, a private one, waiting for water.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this water pump was at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: It is -- well, at that time it was called C5 locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this C5 locality was in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No, it's outside Dobrinja, some 20 minutes away from my flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, is this C5 locality in a district sometimes referred to as the "airport settlement"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were there in the morning of the 12th of July, 1993. Could you tell us from what time did you arrive there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: On Sunday morning, I went to get some water and stood in the queue. That was the 11th of July. And I wait -- June. And I waited for 48 hours. I was wounded, and yet my turn to get water never came.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it from your answer that you went there the day before the 12th, you went there from the 11th of July to wait for water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you carry anything with you in respect to collecting this water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, I had those canisters. That's what we call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall where you were at about 14.45, or 2.45 p.m., on the 12th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I was sitting next to a garage door, in the rear seat of a car. It had been taken out from a car, and it was there. And that is where I was sitting, waiting for my turn to pump water.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say where you were sitting in relation to where the water pump was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: The water pump was in front of me. And I sat -- I was sitting opposite the water pump. The water pump was in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "opposite the water pump"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying as I was sitting, the queue was in front of me, and I was sitting there on the right-hand side. And on the left-hand side was the water pump across the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say where exactly the water pump was across the street from you? Was it on the street or in a yard or in a house? Could you just say where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: In the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was the water pump at the front of the yard, the back of the yard, or the side of the yard? Where was the water pump in respect of the front gate of the yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: There were three steps down which you had to go from the street --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know, we have two screens here on which we can see at times the witness with her face shown, and the other one distorted. I'm just drawing your attention to it. Otherwise, we have no problem with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This has been explained before, that in this courtroom, everyone can see the face of the witness. But outside the courtroom, that's what is shown on the video channel. Yes, please. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking you where in the yard was this water pump. You could start by telling us was it to the front, to the back, or to the side of the yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: In the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did that yard have a gate to enter into the yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you say approximately - you don't need to be exact - just approximately how far the pump was from the gate entering into the yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Well, could have been 3, maybe 4 metres. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said you were waiting for your turn to pump water. Were there other people there waiting for water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in respect to the gate to the yard and the position where the pump was, were there other people there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. A queue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were these people civilians or military personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: They were all civilians. There were no military there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you sat across the street, did anything in particular happen that afternoon? Did you see anything happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I saw when a shell fell and hit a man at the back, the nape of his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you saw when a shell fell. Can you tell us exactly what you saw. Did you see a shell, or could you describe simply what you observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I was sitting, me and my neighbours, and we did not hear the shot. I just felt some heat hit me in the face. And when I looked up, all I could see was blood, flesh, pieces of body flying all over, screams. I never even felt then that I had been wounded, too. It was sheer horror, I mean. Four or five families were, I mean, destroyed or killed. Terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you saw the shell hit a man. Could you describe to us exactly what you mean. Tell us exactly what you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I saw exactly when something hot, white-hot rod, hit him in the neck. When I looked up, he was blown to pieces. There was no way of knowing who it was and how he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say about where this person was standing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: The man was leaning against a gate, the gate of that yard. He was just leaning against it at the moment when the shell fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, I understand it is difficult for you. But I'm going to ask you to recount briefly what you saw and who you saw after this man was blown to pieces. If you need time, you could just take a couple minutes to compose yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No, I don't need a break. I saw -- we were sitting there when the shell fell and blew that man to pieces. I hid under the steps. A mother with two daughters whom I knew, whom I knew well, and their father and husband, he was pumping water. He was wounded, too. I hid -- I went to the left and hid under the steps which were leading into the building. And when this man --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One moment. You said the man was wounded. Do you know what happened to his wife and two daughters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: His wife and one of the daughters were killed on the spot. They were -- their bodies were completely charred. The other daughter lost a leg and an arm, and she died on the way to hospital. And another young woman who was studying, doing her last year of medicine, and her mother, they also died in front of me. A woman who was in front of me, youngish, I think she was all -- the fragments of the shell had pierced, it had punched her body through all over. She was horrible to see. There were 18 dead, 29 wounded. Blood was streaming. It was a horror.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you hid on some stairs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you remain there or did you do anything after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: When the father of those two girls came out, when he came from the pump and when he saw his wife and his daughter, he started screaming. When he saw the other one, he cried out, "Oh, Nagiba [phoen], my child, not you, too." And then I got out from under the stairs. But when I saw all that, I fled to the other yard where everybody else had fled after the shell had fallen. I didn't even realise I had been wounded until a neighbour told me that I was -- that my head was bleeding, that my arm was bleeding. And that neighbour's son put a piece of cloth on my head to stop bleeding, and also bandaged my arm. And then he took me to the asphalt road, and the ambulance car had arrived meanwhile. And I know they put me in that car, and then I fainted. And I knew nothing else. I came to again in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which hospital were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Dobrinja Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were you treated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you admitted or were you discharged that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No, I was immediately admitted into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: For five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you were injured. To what part of your body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: My right arm, above the elbow; my head; and my ribs on the right Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you arrived at Dobrinja Hospital on the 12th of July, at the time of your arrival, were you conscious or unconscious?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: When I arrived in hospital, I came to. I had been unconscious in the ambulance. But when I entered the ambulance, I fainted. But it's very near if you go there by car. It's not very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you came to in the hospital, what did you see there? What was the circumstances in the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: It was terrible. There was no electricity on that day. They were repairing the generator. There were 29 wounded people. They were seriously wounded, people who were more seriously wounded than I was. But we had good doctors there, good specialists, thank goodness. And they treated us. They turned the generator on, and then they started taking care of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, with your leave, may I show the witness Document P3365?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think that document should be on the other side in Sarajevo, but the document has the name of the witness on it, so I would ask if that part be obscured, the name and the address of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Stamp, that none of the pictures of confidential documents will be broadcasted to the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been confirmed to me before this Court session and in the beginning again. So if it's put on the ELMO, it will not be broadcasted out of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness AE, do you see that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the date on it is the 12th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does the document bear your name and address?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And also the year of your birth? Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To the top left hand corner, it says, "General Hospital, Dobrinja, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This document is a medical record in respect to your injury on the 12th of July, 1993, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It could be removed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you, Witness, recall the name of the man whose wife and two daughters died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Rasim. Rasim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of the young lady who had a year to complete her studies, and her mother? Do you recall those names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: The girl, yes, the girl was Stela. But the mother's name, no, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And finally -- not yet, but that day, in the immediate vicinity of where the shell landed, was there any shooting or shelling that day before that shell landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that there was regular shooting and shelling in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: However, you went to this water pump and remained there from the Thursday until -- I beg your pardon. From the 11th until the time it was shelled on the 12th. Can you say why you waited there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: We had to get water from somewhere. We didn't have any water. We had to cook and wash things. It's impossible to live without water.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness AE. Thank you, Mr. President. That will be the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But before I have to ask whether I could be authorised to ask the witness to take her earphones off. This will take a little time. I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that it's something that should be raised before the cross-examination. Okay. Please, Ms. Philpott in Sarajevo, could you take the headphones from the Witness AE. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Let me just ... Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Mr. President, this is the question that I have: The Prosecution has just provided us with a document, 3365, P3365. You have it before you. This document is written in the Serbian language. The Prosecution has added to this a document P3365.1, and this is the translation. Mr. President, if you compare these two documents, and I don't think it's necessary to be a linguist in order to notice this, you will see that the lower part of the diagnosis which finishes with the expression in Serbian "check-up twice a day," this part has not been translated, but it is legible. And you said I was not a doctor, and quite rightly, sir - I can't understand this either in Serbian or in English - but I would appreciate to have a complete translation in English. Would it be possible to provide an entire translation in English so that I can cross-examine the witness in a useful way? Otherwise, I think that yet again we will not be in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, could you explain why there's no full translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- this document is the official translation that we got from the unit responsible. As to why there is no further translation, it does not on its face tell us that. And I don't know if it has anything to do with whether or not there were certain words there which could not be translated. Beyond that, I can't explain further. However, as far as the English version is concerned, I could make inquiries of the CLSS if one could provide it and, if not, why. Looking on the document myself, it seems to indicate -- well, I will not read what it says. But I think the contents of it are pretty clear. And I would need time to give the Court a full translation of these four lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think among those most bothered by not having a translation, perhaps you're not one of them. Since whatever is in the B/C/S language, as we call it, I think you could read it. And so therefore, fortunately Defence is the party who could effectively cross-examine the witness on whatever is there in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you for this remark. But it is up to you to judge and not up to the Defence, and the documents that you will have before you are translations which are not complete. And I ask myself why, what is legible, is not being translated and what is illegible is being translated. So there is a complete confusion here. And the Defence cannot accept this. I will cross-examine this witness, but with the reservation that I will be unaware of certain facts partially or completely. That depends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have two different issues here, I think, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The first is whether the Defence is able to cross-examine the witness; the second is whether the Chamber would finally accept the document without a proper translation. So I think the first question could be answered in a positive way. I think if there's anyone in this courtroom who can read the content of the document, it would be the Defence. So I think the Defence may proceed in cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the other hand, I can imagine that part of the not-translated part is, for example, medication. I could imagine that that is to some extent perhaps the reason why it's not translated. But that's no justification not to translate it. But just in order to assist you, that if you read I think it's general knowledge that, for example, the word penicillin refers to medicaments. If you look at numbers, that is the usual way of writing down what medication a patient should receive. So if it would assist you perhaps for those parts that are not written in B/C/S, I have been glad to do it. So I would now give the opportunity to the Defence to cross-examine the witness. And of course, we have noted your objections against the use of this untranslated document by the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we first ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Ms. Philpott to put the headphone on again. Mrs. AE, you'll now be examined by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Good day to you. Madam Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Witness, you said that, just a minute ago, during the examination-in-chief, that you had seen an object which was warm and which hit a man in the neck. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Madam Witness, at the time of the events, did you know the name of this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, however, you were very categorical, it is a man who is in question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How old was he, more or less, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: About 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, about how many people were waiting - I would like you to remind me of this - in the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Maybe about 50 or 60 people. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like us to be able to visualise this. These people, were they aligned? Were they standing one behind the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: On the same side of the road, Madam Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No. I was sitting on the right side and the line was on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
